top_articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git , migrations , version-control , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , agentic-engineering

top_articles.title_original: LaTeX renderer
top_articles.summary: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 . Tags: latex , paul-ford , tools , urls , ai , generative-ai , llms

top_articles.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.title_original: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

top_articles.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.title_original: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

top_articles.title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.title_original: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 21 日消息，英伟达今日在柏林 GTC 2026 大会上宣布，DGX Spark 此前支持最多 4 台设备组建集群，目前已开放手动配置最多 8 台设备组建集群。如果是以 128GB 版本组建，其统一内存容量最高可达 1TB。 同时，英伟达还发布了本地 AI 平台更新，并宣布与 llama.cpp 、vLLM 开源社区合作优化 AI 推理性能，在特定工作负载下，RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 的推理性能最高提升 40%，DGX Spark 和 DGX Station 也分别获得最高 30% 和 20% 的性能提升。 英伟达表示，4,999 美元 （IT之家注：现汇率约合 33,450 元人民币） 的 DGX Spark 的 64GB 版本将于 10 月 23 日开始通过合作伙伴陆续发售。针对集群部署，英伟达 Sync Model Launcher 计划于本月晚些时候上线，用户可通过该工具下载与硬件配置相匹配的模型和容器，并将模型连接至 OpenCode。工具还将自动加载 DGX Spark Skills，为设备故障排查、维护及工作流程提供指导。 软件更新方面，10 月版 DGX Spark 更新加入 Wi-Fi 助手，允许设备在 appliance mode 下切换无线网络；DGX Spark Skills 也将通过 OpenCode 集成至英伟达 Sync，为日常维护和故障排查提供支持。 模型方面，英伟达宣布支持更多可在本地运行的 AI 模型，包括 Nemotron、GLM、DeepSeek、Qwen、MiniMax 以及 FLUX.3 Klein 等，覆盖智能体、编程、图像生成和编辑等任务。 英伟达还推出针对本地 AI 硬件优化的 Recursive Flint 编程模型。该模型采用混合专家（MoE）架构，总参数量为 400 亿，激活参数量为 25 亿。英伟达称，该模型在配备 64GB 内存的 RTX Spark 上推理速度超过每秒 220 个词元。 针对本地运行大型模型时的内存压力，英伟达还发布了一组优化内存使用的模型检查点，通过量化降低内存占用，同时尽可能保持接近全精度模型的准确性。其中， Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local 可在单台 128GB DGX Spark 或 RTX PRO 6000 上运行；GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local 则面向两台系统的配置。 推理性能优化是此次更新的另一项重点。根据英伟达公布的数据，在 llama.cpp 中，针对 Qwen 3.8 Flash Next 的多 token 预测（MTP）推测解码优化，可使 RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 上的端到端智能体任务提速最高 1.4 倍；在 vLLM 中，针对 Qwen3.8 27B 的推测解码和 FlashInfer 预填充内核优化，可使 DGX Spark 上的相关任务提速最高 1.3 倍；DGX Station 运行 GLM 5.3 Flash 时，吞吐量最高提升至原来的 1.2 倍。 英伟达还公布了 DGX Station 的企业管理与应用扩展计划，包括新增 Absolute Security、思科旗下 Splunk、Microsoft Intune、Tanium 等七项管理集成，帮助企业部署和管理本地 AI 基础设施。 DGX Station 的 Windows 版本预计于 12 月推出，将支持制造业相关应用，以及设计、仿真、验证和工程自动化工作流。 此外，英伟达计划为 DGX Station 推出开放源代码机器人参考工作流，并以早期访问形式提供 NVIDIA Cloud Functions，让团队通过统一接口共享本地模型服务。 相关阅读： 《 英伟达黄仁勋：已测超 1200 款应用，RTX Spark 是全球唯一本地原生运行所有应用的电脑 》 《 桌面 AI 超算新选择：英伟达 NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB 内存版正式发布，4999 美元 》

top_articles.title_original: 报告称 2026 年国内大模型均价翻倍，每秒吞吐量也翻倍
top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 23 日消息，中国信息通信研究院（简称“中国信通院”）人工智能研究所、人工智能大模型及软硬件评测工业和信息化部重点实验室和中国人工智能产业发展联盟，今日（10 月 23 日）联合发布《大模型词元服务性能监测报告（2026 年）》。 报告称，随着大模型技术的迅速迭代，词元（Token）服务成为从技术走向应用的关键点，我国日均词元调用量持续攀升， 2026 年 6 月，国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍 。 产业中越来越多的 MaaS（Model as a Service，模型即服务）平台厂商通过公有云 API 方式供给大模型词元服务。然而用户对词元服务性能缺乏直观的判断依据， 且面临选型困难等各类问题 。 报告基于 2026 年 1-8 月的监测数据，围绕各平台词元服务调用成功率、吞吐速度、首词时延、稳定性、价格、上下文窗口等维度开展分析，对比原厂大模型官方平台，以及 DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM、Kimi 四款开源模型在第三方平台上的性能差异，进一步分析影响词元服务性能的关键因素，总结产业核心观察，明确下一步工作计划，旨在为用户选型提供参考，并为产业界优化服务能力提供方向指引。 1. 国内词元服务每秒吞吐量较 2025 年翻倍，仍低于国外 报告提出，8 月份国内各模型平均 TPS（每秒输出词元数）达到 78.23（个 / 秒）， 与 2025 年均值 38.25（个 / 秒）相比实现翻倍 。但 8 月份国外典型模型的 TPS 均值为 112.82（个 / 秒），与 2025 年 12 月的 51.35（个 / 秒）相比，提升亦超过一倍，整体优于国内。 所有大模型词元服务月均 TPS 2. 词元服务时延有所增加，国内外趋势一致 报告提出，今年以来，国内各模型的平均 TTFT（首词时延）呈现持续提升态势，8 月份均值达到 1.26 秒， 相较于 2025 年平均值 0.78 秒明显增加 。但同时 8 月份国外典型模型 TTFT 平均值达到 2.08 秒，相比 4 月份 1.04 秒亦明显增加。 值得注意的是，TTFT 上升并非单纯的性能退化，而是伴随着模型参数量增加、上下文长度增加、调用量增加等多种因素同步产生的结果。 所有大模型词元服务的月均 TTFT 3. 2026 年词元服务价格明显回升 报告提出，经历了过去两年价格战后，2026 年国内外模型服务价格明显上涨。 国内 2025 下半年归一化均价为 6.8 元，而今年以来均价为 13.46 元，涨幅接近 1 倍 。但国外价格仍高于国内，2026 年以来发布的典型模型平均归一价格约为 117.8 元。 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 4. 模型上下文长度不断向百万级长度扩展 报告提出，被监测的模型中，上下文长度达到 1M（1 百万词元）的模型占比 47.8%，200K 及以上的合计达 95.7%，相比 2025 年底的占比提高超过 76 个百分点，而低于 200K 的模型占比持续减少。 国内大模型上下文长度占比情况 5. 开源模型词元服务性能提升显著，同一模型在不同平台性能波动较大 报告提出，5 月份更新了 4 款开源模型的新版本进行监测，结果显示 TPS 持续提升，TTFT 时延不断压缩。例如 8 月份 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 的 TPS 已达到 DeepSeek-V3.2 的 2 倍。 时延方面，5 月份主要模型完成换代升级后，TTFT 普遍出现阶段性上升，随着推理优化措施落地，时延指标逐步回落至换代前水平。 同时， 4 款模型在不同平台上的 TPS、TTFT、调用成功率表现不一 。部分第三方平台性能明显优于官方平台提供的模型服务，同一模型在不同平台间的 TPS 差距最大可接近一倍。各平台对相同模型的推理加速、优化策略、成本控制不同，是造成性能分化的主要原因。 开源模型性能综合对比图

top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 21 日消息，英伟达当地时间 10 月 21 日在 GTC 柏林大会上宣布扩展 Isaac 开放机器人开发平台，新增人形机器人参考平台、运行框架、仿真资产和数据集，并更新机器人学习工具，覆盖从训练数据生成、仿真训练到实体机器人部署的开发流程。 硬件方面，英伟达联合思灵机器人（Agile Robots）发布了人形机器人参考平台 Agile ONE SN，计划于 2027 年初推出。 该平台预配置英伟达 Isaac GR00T，并搭载 Jetson Thor 计算平台，主要面向机器人研究与开发。通过整合仿真、训练和部署工具，Agile Robots 表示，该平台可将相关环境的前期配置时间从数周缩短至数天。 英伟达创始人兼 CEO 黄仁勋表示，通用机器人技术正在快速发展，机器人领域的“ChatGPT 时刻”正加速到来。英伟达称，此次更新旨在为开发者提供模型、数据、仿真工具和计算系统，帮助他们将通用机器人技术应用于实际产业场景。 思灵机器人 Agile ONE SN 采用 Agile ONE S 人形机器人本体，身高 1.4 米、重量 40 公斤，具有 31 个自由度，单臂负载为 3 公斤。其配备两只 WUJI Hand 2 五指灵巧手，每只手具有 20 个自由度，支持 1kHz 力控制和触觉感知。需要注意的是，路透社报道该机器人重量约为 34 公斤，与英伟达官方公布的 40 公斤数据存在差异，现有信息尚不足以确认差异原因。 计算方面，Agile ONE SN 搭载英伟达 Jetson Thor，提供 2070 TFLOPS 的 FP4 算力和 128GB 统一内存。传感器包括头部及腕部摄像头、激光雷达和惯性测量单元，用于感知周围环境并支持机器人与外部环境交互。 安全方面，该平台计划将机器人端安全协议与英伟达 Halos 全栈安全系统集成，目前这项集成仍待完成。英伟达表示，斯坦福大学、苏黎世联邦理工学院等研究机构已对 Agile ONE SN 表示兴趣。 路透社另报道称，Agile Robots 计划于 2027 年与英伟达合作生产最多 2000 台人形机器人，面向大学和企业研究实验室等客户。 软件方面，英伟达 Isaac Lab 3.0 已正式发布，作为开源机器人学习框架，支持多 GPU 训练工作流，并可使用 Newton、PhysX 等物理引擎。该框架旨在帮助开发者训练和优化机器人策略，覆盖从桌面工作站到数据中心的不同计算环境。 IT之家注意到，英伟达还推出开源运行框架 Isaac OS。该框架基于 Holoscan 构建，用于连接 AI 模型、传感器、控制系统和机器人硬件，支持从仿真环境迁移至实体机器人，并提供确定性实时运行能力。 针对 DGX Station，英伟达同时发布了三套开源参考工作流。第一套通过强化学习优化 GR00T 1.7 模型；第二套利用 Isaac Lab 训练灵巧操作技能；第三套则借助 ChatGPT Astra 对 Cosmos 世界模型进行后训练，以生成合成训练数据。这些工作流旨在帮助开发者整合机器人学习、仿真和数据生成环节。 数据方面，SimReady Central Library 提供超过 2000 项可用于仿真的机器人和工厂资产，涵盖多种机器人设备及工业场景资源。Human 1M 数据集则包含多种人类活动、同步三视角视频和三维手部追踪数据，可用于机器人学习与动作理解。两项资源均通过 Hugging Face 提供，其中完整版本的 Human 1M 数据集仅向 Cosmos Coalition 合作伙伴开放。 英伟达还介绍了多家采用其机器人开发工具的企业。ABB Robotics 将 Omniverse 库整合至 RobotStudio HyperReality，用于机器人系统安装前的仿真和虚拟调试；NEURA Robotics 则利用 Isaac Sim 和 Isaac Lab 生成合成训练数据，并在仿真环境中训练机器人技能。英伟达表示，KUKA、Humanoid、Sereact 和 Universal Robots 等企业也在采用其开放机器人平台相关技术。

top_articles.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

top_articles.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.

top_articles.title: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents
top_articles.title_original: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many Indian banks serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots. Assistants based on language models could respond faster and carry out requests such as blocking a card, but only if they give correct information and follow the bank's rules. These rules prescribe a procedure, a set of required steps, such as obtaining a closure quote before closing a deposit. Adapting models to this domain requires measuring how well they follow the procedure, before and after training. Benchmarks usually judge only the records left at the end of a conversation. Many required steps, however, leave the records unchanged, so an assistant that skips them can still be judged successful. We present TauIndianBankBench, an action-oriented benchmark of 1,000 Indian retail-banking tasks where an assistant helps a simulated customer. Besides the final records, it checks that the assistant took every required step and made no unrequested change. For every model, 6.5-12.0% of sessions are judged successful when only the final records are checked, although the assistant skipped a required step or made an unrequested change. Scoring both procedure and outcome shows more accurately how well language models perform in Indian retail banking.

top_articles.title: Measure First, Then Allocate: Calibrated Rollout Budgets for MCP Agents in Reinforcement Learning
top_articles.title_original: Measure First, Then Allocate: Calibrated Rollout Budgets for MCP Agents in Reinforcement Learning
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training tool-using language models requires costly interaction, yet identical rewards within a rollout group provide no group-relative learning signal. We use reward disagreement to guide harness evaluation and the allocation of rollouts for policy training in Model Context Protocol (MCP) environments. We first introduce Discord, which tests harness edits using exact paired inference and decision-preserving early stopping: only disagreeing paired outcomes favor one harness over another. This insight motivates prospective allocation in BRACE (Bank-calibrated Rollout Allocation under Correlated Episodes). BRACE combines historical task evidence, uncertainty in task success rates, and a correlated reward model to forecast mixed-reward groups before allocating generation budget. Controlled harness experiments favor Discord, while live MCP experiments expose a retention-cost trade-off. At three Qwen3-VL model scales, BRACE exceeds the strongest plotted baseline peaks with fewer new training rollouts; historical-bank collection is counted separately. It also leads the compared methods on BFCL and NESTFUL without further training. Ablations probe the bank, estimator, and allocation score; prospective evaluation checks forecast calibration. These results support forecasting reward contrast before generation.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.title_original: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

top_articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. top_articles.summary: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . top_articles.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.title_original: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

top_articles.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.title_original: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

top_articles.title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.title_original: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 23 日消息，中国信息通信研究院（简称“中国信通院”）人工智能研究所、人工智能大模型及软硬件评测工业和信息化部重点实验室和中国人工智能产业发展联盟，今日（10 月 23 日）联合发布《大模型词元服务性能监测报告（2026 年）》。 报告称，随着大模型技术的迅速迭代，词元（Token）服务成为从技术走向应用的关键点，我国日均词元调用量持续攀升， 2026 年 6 月，国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍 。 产业中越来越多的 MaaS（Model as a Service，模型即服务）平台厂商通过公有云 API 方式供给大模型词元服务。然而用户对词元服务性能缺乏直观的判断依据， 且面临选型困难等各类问题 。 报告基于 2026 年 1-8 月的监测数据，围绕各平台词元服务调用成功率、吞吐速度、首词时延、稳定性、价格、上下文窗口等维度开展分析，对比原厂大模型官方平台，以及 DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM、Kimi 四款开源模型在第三方平台上的性能差异，进一步分析影响词元服务性能的关键因素，总结产业核心观察，明确下一步工作计划，旨在为用户选型提供参考，并为产业界优化服务能力提供方向指引。 1. 国内词元服务每秒吞吐量较 2025 年翻倍，仍低于国外 报告提出，8 月份国内各模型平均 TPS（每秒输出词元数）达到 78.23（个 / 秒）， 与 2025 年均值 38.25（个 / 秒）相比实现翻倍 。但 8 月份国外典型模型的 TPS 均值为 112.82（个 / 秒），与 2025 年 12 月的 51.35（个 / 秒）相比，提升亦超过一倍，整体优于国内。 所有大模型词元服务月均 TPS 2. 词元服务时延有所增加，国内外趋势一致 报告提出，今年以来，国内各模型的平均 TTFT（首词时延）呈现持续提升态势，8 月份均值达到 1.26 秒， 相较于 2025 年平均值 0.78 秒明显增加 。但同时 8 月份国外典型模型 TTFT 平均值达到 2.08 秒，相比 4 月份 1.04 秒亦明显增加。 值得注意的是，TTFT 上升并非单纯的性能退化，而是伴随着模型参数量增加、上下文长度增加、调用量增加等多种因素同步产生的结果。 所有大模型词元服务的月均 TTFT 3. 2026 年词元服务价格明显回升 报告提出，经历了过去两年价格战后，2026 年国内外模型服务价格明显上涨。 国内 2025 下半年归一化均价为 6.8 元，而今年以来均价为 13.46 元，涨幅接近 1 倍 。但国外价格仍高于国内，2026 年以来发布的典型模型平均归一价格约为 117.8 元。 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 4. 模型上下文长度不断向百万级长度扩展 报告提出，被监测的模型中，上下文长度达到 1M（1 百万词元）的模型占比 47.8%，200K 及以上的合计达 95.7%，相比 2025 年底的占比提高超过 76 个百分点，而低于 200K 的模型占比持续减少。 国内大模型上下文长度占比情况 5. 开源模型词元服务性能提升显著，同一模型在不同平台性能波动较大 报告提出，5 月份更新了 4 款开源模型的新版本进行监测，结果显示 TPS 持续提升，TTFT 时延不断压缩。例如 8 月份 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 的 TPS 已达到 DeepSeek-V3.2 的 2 倍。 时延方面，5 月份主要模型完成换代升级后，TTFT 普遍出现阶段性上升，随着推理优化措施落地，时延指标逐步回落至换代前水平。 同时， 4 款模型在不同平台上的 TPS、TTFT、调用成功率表现不一 。部分第三方平台性能明显优于官方平台提供的模型服务，同一模型在不同平台间的 TPS 差距最大可接近一倍。各平台对相同模型的推理加速、优化策略、成本控制不同，是造成性能分化的主要原因。 开源模型性能综合对比图

top_articles.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

top_articles.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.

top_articles.title: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents
top_articles.title_original: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many Indian banks serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots. Assistants based on language models could respond faster and carry out requests such as blocking a card, but only if they give correct information and follow the bank's rules. These rules prescribe a procedure, a set of required steps, such as obtaining a closure quote before closing a deposit. Adapting models to this domain requires measuring how well they follow the procedure, before and after training. Benchmarks usually judge only the records left at the end of a conversation. Many required steps, however, leave the records unchanged, so an assistant that skips them can still be judged successful. We present TauIndianBankBench, an action-oriented benchmark of 1,000 Indian retail-banking tasks where an assistant helps a simulated customer. Besides the final records, it checks that the assistant took every required step and made no unrequested change. For every model, 6.5-12.0% of sessions are judged successful when only the final records are checked, although the assistant skipped a required step or made an unrequested change. Scoring both procedure and outcome shows more accurately how well language models perform in Indian retail banking.

top_articles.title: Measure First, Then Allocate: Calibrated Rollout Budgets for MCP Agents in Reinforcement Learning
top_articles.title_original: Measure First, Then Allocate: Calibrated Rollout Budgets for MCP Agents in Reinforcement Learning
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training tool-using language models requires costly interaction, yet identical rewards within a rollout group provide no group-relative learning signal. We use reward disagreement to guide harness evaluation and the allocation of rollouts for policy training in Model Context Protocol (MCP) environments. We first introduce Discord, which tests harness edits using exact paired inference and decision-preserving early stopping: only disagreeing paired outcomes favor one harness over another. This insight motivates prospective allocation in BRACE (Bank-calibrated Rollout Allocation under Correlated Episodes). BRACE combines historical task evidence, uncertainty in task success rates, and a correlated reward model to forecast mixed-reward groups before allocating generation budget. Controlled harness experiments favor Discord, while live MCP experiments expose a retention-cost trade-off. At three Qwen3-VL model scales, BRACE exceeds the strongest plotted baseline peaks with fewer new training rollouts; historical-bank collection is counted separately. It also leads the compared methods on BFCL and NESTFUL without further training. Ablations probe the bank, estimator, and allocation score; prospective evaluation checks forecast calibration. These results support forecasting reward contrast before generation.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.title_original: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.
